readings.c1s1:
¶
'''wormpipe''' (wėrm′pīp), ''n.'' The worm of a still.
{{smaller block|The gas then in its passage through the ''worm-pipe'' of the condenser (which is always surrounded with cold water) is condensed.{{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 727.}}}}

'''worm-powder''' (wėrm′pou″dėr), ''n.'' A powder used for expelling worms from the intestinal canal or other open cavities of the body.

'''worm-punch''' (wėrm′punch), ''n.'' A small, rather slender punch, used by coopers for clearing out worm-holes in staves or heads of casks, for the purpose of stopping the holes with wooden plugs to prevent leaking.

'''worm-rack''' (wėrm′rak), ''n.'' A rack gearing with a worm-wheel. The teeth are set obliquely, corresponding in obliquity with the pitch of the worm. See cut under ''rack''<sup>1</sup>, 6.

'''worm-safe''' (wėrm′sāf), ''n.'' A locked chamber containing a hydrometer, and attached to the worm of a still in such manner that a fractional part of the liquor distilled trickles into it from the worm. The mean specific gravity of the liquor is indicated by the hydrometer.

'''wormseed''' (wėrm′sēd), ''n.'' '''1.''' Same as ''santonica''. See ''santonica'' and ''santonin''.
{{smaller block|''Worme-seede'' [cometh] from Persia.{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. i. 278.}}}}
'''2.''' The fruit of the American herb ''Chenopodium ambrosioides'', especially var. ''anthelminticum'', which is often reckoned a distinct species; also
readings.c1s2:
¶
the plant itself. {{smaller|The seed is an officinal as well as a popular vermifuge. It yields wormseed-oil (which see), and is also given in the form of a powder. Distinguished as ''American wormseed''; also called ''Mexican tea''.}} '''3.''' The treacle-mustard, ''Erysimum cheiranthoides'', or primarily its seed, which was formerly a popular vermifuge in England. Also ''treacle wormseed''.—{{smaller|'''American wormseed.''' See def. 2.—'''Barbary wormseed,''' the heads of species of ''Artemisia'' growing in Syria and Arabia, used like santonica.—'''Levant wormseed.''' See ''santonica''.—'''Oil of wormseed.''' See ''oil'' and ''wormseed-oil''.—'''Spanish wormseed,''' a chenopodiaceous plant, ''Salsola'' (''Halogeton, Caroxylon'') ''tamariscifolia'', or particularly its seed, which is used as an anthelmintic.—'''Treacle-wormseed.''' See def. 3.}}

'''wormseed-mustard''' (wėrm′sēd-mus″tärd), ''n.'' See ''mustard''.

'''wormseed-oil''' (werm′sēd-oil), ''n.'' A volatile oil obtained from wormseed. It is probably without active medicinal properties.

'''worm-shaft''' (wėrm′shȧft), ''n.'' The screw-threaded shaft which engages the teeth of a worm-gear or worm-wheel.

'''worm-shaped''' (wėrm′shāpt), ''a.'' Having the form of a worm; vermiform; vermicular.

'''worm-shell''' (wėrm′shel), ''n.'' A mollusk of the family ''Vermetidæ'', or its shell: so called from the long twisted or vermiform shape of the shell. See cut under ''Vermetus''.

'''worms’-meat''' (wėrmz′mēt), ''n.'' Food for worms; dead flesh. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I am dead
Already, girl; and so is she and he;
We are all ''worms’-meat'' now.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v.}}}}

'''worm-snake''' (wėrm′snāk), ''n.'' '''1.''' A blindwor a worm-like angiostomatous or scolecophidi snake of the suborder ''Typhlopoidea''; a groun snake, as ''Carphophis'' (or ''Celuta'') ''amœna''.— Same as ''snakeworm''.

'''worm-tea''' (wėrm′tē), ''n.'' A decoction of so plant, generally a bitter plant, used as anthelmintic.

'''worm-track''' (wėrm′trak), ''n.'' Same as ''wor cast'', 2.

'''wormul''' (wôr′mul), ''n.'' Same as ''warble''<sup>3</sup>.

'''worm-wheel''' (wėrm′hwēl), ''n.'' A wheel whi gears with an endless or tangent screw or wor receiving or imparting motion. {{smaller|By this mear powerful effect with a diminished rate of motion is co municated from one revolving shaft to another. ''tangent screw'' (under ''tangent''), ''endless screw'' (under ''endl'' with cut); also cuts under ''Hindley’s screw'' (at ''screw'') under ''steam-engine''.}}

'''wormwood''' (wėrm′wu̇d), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wormw'' an altered form, simulating ''worm'' + ''wood''<sup>1</sup>, the earlier ''wermode'', ''wermod'', ''wormod'', < ''wermod'' = MD. ''wermoed'', ''wermoet'', ''wermōt'', ''w mōde'', ''wermēde'', ''warmōt'', ''warmōde'', etc., = OE

''wehren,'' et defend, protect, keep, + ''mōd,'' mood, mind: ''wear''<sup>2</sup> and ''mood''<sup>1</sup>.] A somewhat woody per nial herb, ''Artemisia Absinthium,'' native in rope and Asiatic Russia, found in old gard
readings.c2s1:
and by roadsides in North America. {{smaller|This plant is proverbial for its bitterness, and was in medicinal use among the ancients. It is of a highly tonic property, and is still used in Europe for weak digestion; it was formerly employed for intermittents and some other troubles, and was once regarded as a vermifuge. It is very largely consumed, with a few other species, in preparing the absinthe beverage of the French. (See ''absinthe'' and ''absinthium'' (with cut)). The name is extended to the genus, or particularly to species closely related to this; various species have their own names, as ''southernwood'', ''mugwort'', ''tarragon'', ''santonica'', and ''sage-brush''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The soure Almaunde, & ''wermode'', & feyn greeke,
Frote hem yfere asmoche as wol suffice.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 196.}}
<poem>These for frenzy be
A speedy and a sovereign remedy,
The bitter ''wormwood'', sage, and marigold.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, ii. 2.}}}}
Figuratively—'''2.''' Bitterness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Weed this ''wormwood'' from your fruitful brain.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 857.}}
<poem>Sir, with this truth
You mix such ''wormwood'' that you leave no hope
For my disorder’d palate e’er to relish
A wholesome taste again. ''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, i. 2.</poem>
His presence and his communications were gall and ''wormwood'' to his once partial mistress.
{{right|''Scott'', Kenilworth, xi.}}}}

¶
'''worowe†''', ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''worry''.

'''worpe†''', '''worpare†'''. Old spellings of ''warp'', ''warper''.

'''worret''' (wur′et), ''v.'' See ''worrit''.

'''worricow''' (wur′i-kou), ''n.'' [Sc., also spelled ''worrycow'' and ''wirrycow''; < ''worry'' + ''cow'', a goblin, scarecrow.] '''1.''' A hobgoblin; the devil.
{{smaller block|''Worricows'' and gyre-carlins that haunted about the auld wa’s at e’en.
{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxi.}}}}
'''2.''' Any frightful object; an ugly, awkward-looking person; a fright; a bugbear; a scarecrow.
{{smaller block|What a ''worricrow'' the man doth look!
{{right|''Naylor'', Reynard the Fox, 39. (''Davies.'')}}}}
[Scotch in both uses.]

'''worrier''' (wur′i-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''worry'', ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who worries or harasses (himself or others); one who is given to worrying or who harasses with anxious forebodings.
{{smaller block|The ''worriers'' of souls.
{{right|''J. Spencer'', Prodigies, p. 229.}}}}

'''worriless''' (wur′i-les), ''a.'' [< ''worry'' + ''-less''.] Free from worry.
{{smaller block|The professor, leading a comparatively congenial and ''worriless'' life, is a deeper sleeper and a less frequent dreamer [than the teacher].
{{right|''Science'', XIII. 88.}}}}

'''worriment''' (wur′i-mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''worry'' + ''-ment''.] Trouble; anxiety; worry. [Colloq.]

'''worrisome''' (wur′i-sum), ''a.'' [< ''worry'' + ''-some''.] Causing worry or annoyance; troublesome.
{{smaller block|I must give orders . . . that you come in at once with that ''worrisome'' cough of yours.
{{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, xlv.}}}}

'''worrit''' (wur′it), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' [Also ''worret''; a dial. form, with excrescent ''t'', of ''worry'', ''v.''] To worry.
readings.c3s4:
(see ''tease''), disturb, disquiet.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To choke; be suffocated, as by something stopping the windpipe. [Obsolete or Scotch.]

{{smaller block|'''Biennial wormwood''', ''Artemisia biennis'', a weed of the interior northern United States, now spreading eastward. It grows from 1 to 3 feet high, and has once- or twice-pinnatifid leaves, with numerous small greenish heads crowded in their axils.—'''Oil of wormwood''', a volatile oil distilled from the common wormwood, usually of a dark-green color, containing the property of the herb.—'''Roman wormwood.''' (''a'') ''Artemisia Pontica'', an Old World species, more aromatic and less bitter than the common wormwood, preferred in Roman medicine, but now scarcely used. (''b'') By transference of the name, the common ragweed, ''Ambrosia artemisiæfolia'', a bitter plant with foliage dissected somewhat like that of an artemisia.—'''Salt of wormwood.''' See ''salt''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Sea wormwood''', the European ''Artemisia maritima''.—'''Silver wormwood''', ''Artemisia argentea'', a silvery silky shrub of Madeira.—'''Tartarian wormwood.''' Same as ''santonica'', 1.—'''Tree-wormwood''', ''Artemisia arborescens'', an erect tree-like species found on rocky shores and islands of the Mediterranean.—'''Wild wormwood''' of the West Indies. See ''Parthenium''.—'''Wormwood wine''', wine which has received a bitter taste from having artemisia steeped in it. Compare ''vermouth''.}}

'''wormwood-moth''' (wėrm′wu̇d-môth), ''n.'' A rare British noctuid, ''Cucullia absinthii.'' {{smaller|It is gray with black spots, and its larva feeds on wormwood. It is found chiefly in Devonshire and Cornwall.}}

'''wormwood-pug''' (wėrm′wu̇d-pug), ''n.'' A British geometrid moth, ''Eupithecia absinthiata'', whose larva feeds upon wormwood.

'''wormy''' (wėr′mi), ''a.''   [< ''worm'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Containing a worm; full of worms; infested or affected with worms; lousy, as fish; measly, as pork; worm-eaten, as timber, fruit, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>Damned spirits all . . .
Already to their ''wormy'' beds are gone.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'' M. N. D., iii. 2. 384.}}}}
'''2.''' Worm-like; low; mean; debased; groveling; earthy. {{smaller block|Sordid and ''wormy'' affections.
{{right|''Bp. Reynolds'', The Passions, xxxvii. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''3.''' Associated with earthworms, and hence with the earth or the grave; gloomy or dismal as the grave. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A weary ''wormy'' darkness.
{{right|''Mrs. Browning.''}}}}

'''worn''' (wōrn), ''p. a.''   [Pp. of ''wear''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Impaired or otherwise affected by wear or use.
{{smaller block|As she trode along the foot-''worn'' passages, and opened one crazy door after another, and ascended the creaking stair-case, she gazed wistfully and fearfully around.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xvi.}}}}

'''2.''' Spent; passed.
{{smaller block|This is but a day, and ’tis well ''worn'' too now.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iv. 2.}}}}

'''3.''' Wearied; exhausted; showing signs of care, illness, fatigue, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy ''worn'' form pursues me night and day,
Smiling reproach.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Prometheus Unbound, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The old ''worn'' world of hurry and heat.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Invitation.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Lead the ''worn'' war-horse by the plumèd bier—
Even his horse, now he is dead, is dear.</poem>
{{right|''T. B. Aldrich'', Landor.}}}}

'''wornal, wornil''' (wôr′na̤l, -nil), ''n.'' Same as ''wormal.'' See ''warble''<sup>3</sup>.

'''worn-out''' (wōrn′out), ''a.'' '''1.''' So much injured by wear as to be unfit for use: as, a ''worn-out'' coat or hat.—'''2.''' Wearied; exhausted, as with toil.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''worn-out'' clerk</poem> Brow-beats his desk below.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Sonnet to J. M. K.}}}}
'''3.''' Past; gone; removed; departed.
{{smaller block|This pattern of the ''worn-out'' age.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 135}}}}
{{smaller block|Pehor also, and Bael-pehor, and the rest, whose Rit are now rotten, and the memorie ''worne out.''
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 9}}}}

'''worrit''' (wur′it), ''v. t.'' and ''i.''   [Also ''worret''; a dial. form, with excrescent ''t'', of ''worry'', ''v.'']   To worry. [Colloq. or slang.]

{{smaller block|I don’t tell everything to your papa. I should only ''worrit'' him and vex him.{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xxiv.}}}}

{{smaller block|Why, father, how you keep on ''worriting!''{{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, I. vii.}}}}

'''worrit''' (wur′it), ''n.''   [< ''worrit, v.'']   Worry; annoyance; vexation. [Colloq. or slang.]

{{smaller block|“Mrs. Richards’s eldest, Miss!” said Susan, “and the ''worrit'' of Mrs. Richards’s life!”{{right|''Dickens'', Dombey and Son, xxiii.}}}}

'''worry''' (wur′i), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''worried'', ppr. ''worrying''.   [< ME. *''worryen, wirryen, wyryen, wirien, worowen, worewen, wirwen, *wurȝen'', < AS. ''wyrgan'', found in comp. ''āwyrgan'', harm, = OFries. ''wergia, wirgia'' = MD. ''worghen'', D. ''worgen, wurgen'' = MLG. LG. ''worgen'' = OHG. ''wurgan'', MHG. G. ''würgen'', strangle, suffocate, choke; cf. AS. ''wearh, wearg, werg'', a wolf, outlaw (''wyrgen'', f., she-wolf, in comp. ''grundwyrgen''), = MHG. ''warc'' = Icel. ''vargr'', wolf, outlaw, accursed person; cf. AS. ''wyrgan, wyrigan, wergian, wergean'', > ME. ''warien'', curse: see ''warry, v., warriangle'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To choke; suffocate. [Now only Scotch.]

<poem>His owen kynde briddis,
That weren anoyed in his nest and norished ffull ille,
And well ny ''yworewid'' with a wronge leder.</poem>{{right|''Richard the Redeless'', iii. 72.}}

{{smaller block|The reek will ''worrie'' me.{{right|''Loudoun Castle'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 256).}}}}

'''2.''' To seize by the throat with the teeth; bite at or tear with the teeth, as dogs when fighting; kill or injure badly by repeated biting, tearing, shaking, etc.: as, a dog that ''worries'' sheep; a terrier ''worries'' rats.
{{smaller block|Wolues that ''wyryeth'' men, wommen, and children.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), x. 226.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A hell-hound that doth hunt us all to death;
That dog that hath his teeth before his eyes,
To ''worry'' lambs, and lap their gentle blood.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 50.}}}}

'''3.''' To tease; trouble; harass with importunity or with care and anxiety; plague; bother; vex; persecute.
{{smaller block|If departed of his own accord, like that lost sheep (Luke 15. 4, &c.), the true church either with her own or any borrowd force ''worries'' him not in again, but rather in all charitable manner sends after him. {{right|''Milton'', Civil Power.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let them rail,
And ''worry'' one another at their pleasure.</poem>
{{right|''Rowe.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ghastly dun shall ''worry'' his sleep.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Reflections of a Proud Pedestrian.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To worry down''', to swallow or put down by a strong effort of the will. [Colloq.]}}
{{smaller block|She ''worried down'' the tea, and ate a slice of toast.
{{right|''E. E. Hale'', Ten Times One, iv.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To worry the sword''', in ''fencing'', to fret one’s opponent by small movements in rapid succession which seem about to result in thrusts or feints. The object is to disconcert him until his guard becomes open or weak, and a thrust can be delivered with effect. ='''Syn. 3.''' ''Pester'', ''Plague'', etc.}} (see ''tease''), disturb, disquiet.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To choke; be suffocated, as by something stopping the windpipe. [Obsolete or Scotch.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
